newsitem.title: USA: Columbia/HCA officials plead not guilty.
newsitem.headline: Columbia/HCA officials plead not guilty.

text.p: Three executives with Columbia/HCA Healthcare Corp pleaded not guilty Tuesday to charges that they defrauded Medicare by overbilling $1.77 million.

The defendants made no comment except to answer "Yes" when U.S. Magistrate George Swartz asked whether they understood the charges and the potential penalty. Their lawyers entered the not guilty pleas.

Robert Whiteside, director of reimbursements at Columbia headquarters in Nashville, Tenn.; Michael Neeb, chief financial officer in the firm's northern Florida division; and Jay Jarrell, chief executive in the company's southwest Florida region, are each charged with five counts of conspiracy and fraud.

The indictment alleges they defrauded the federal government by overbilling the Medicare program and the program that provides health insurance for military families, the Civilian Health and Medical Program.
Swartz sought to ensure that none of the defendants' lawyers had potential conflicts of interest if they were being paid by Columbia.
"I am told Columbia Healthcare hospital, whatever, is a target of the investigation," Swartz told the defendants. "Their defense could be in conflict with your defense."
None of the attorneys disclosed who was paying their bills. However, all three assured that they had no potential conflict.
Sam Jacobson, representing Whiteside, said: "As far as we're concerned, his employer is nonexistent."
"We don't perceive any conflict," he added.
Peter George, attorney for Jarrell, reiterated that sentiment. "I have no loyalties to anyone other than Mr. Jarrell."

The judge ordered prosecutors to turn over to the defense lawyers any evidentiary documents they asked for and set a hearing for September 4 to check progress. Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathleen Haley said the documents would not be made public.
If convicted, each faces up to 25 years in prison and fines of up to $1.25 million.
Columbia/HCA is the nation's largest for-profit hospital chain and is based in Nashville, Tenn. It owns 67 Florida hospitals, accounting for one-third of the hospital beds in the state.

Federal investigators are probing its Medicare billing procedures and its incentive plans for doctors. Separately, Florida and other states have launched local probes of its Medicare billing practices. State pension managers in New York, Florida and Louisiana also have filed civil lawsuits against the company, alleging its managers endangered the value of the stock held in public retirement funds.
